findings.title: Remove unverified curl|sh remote script execution from image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN step downloads https://example.com/install.sh over TLS only and pipes it directly to sh with no version pin, checksum, or signature verification. Whoever controls that URL (or a MITM if TLS is ever bypassed/downgraded, or the domain is re-registered/serves different content later) executes arbitrary code inside every image build, permanently baking the payload into the shipped image. Additionally, curl -sL lacks --fail, so a 404/500 response body is still piped to sh, turning an HTTP error into silent garbage execution rather than a clean build failure.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget goroutines remove completion signal and can leak or panic
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every result was sent, so a caller could safely do `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` or rely on return as completion. Now Run returns immediately while goroutines block on `results <-`. Any caller that closes the channel after Run returns gets a send-on-closed-channel panic; any caller that stops reading before len(jobs) results (early exit, error, cancellation) leaks the remaining goroutines forever, since ctx is never consulted and the send never unblocks. The exported function now has no way to observe completion or failure-to-send.

findings.title: Log() accepts tag parameter but never uses it, silently dropping caller data
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `Log(message string, tag ...string)` promises tagging behavior, but the body is `println(message)` and never references `tag`. Any caller passing `Log("msg", "urgent")` gets output identical to `Log("msg")` — the tag is silently discarded with no error, so callers cannot distinguish 'tag applied' from 'tag dropped'. Per Trigger C, a public parameter promising behavior the body does not implement is a defect in the shipped contract itself, independent of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Permission check widened: any tenant member can delete any record
findings.whyItBreaks: Old predicate required isAdmin AND same-tenant. Substituting a non-admin session (isAdmin=false, tenantId=T) against a record owned by someone else (tenantId=T, ownerId≠session.userId): old = false && true = denied; new = false || true = allowed. Every regular user can now delete every record in their tenant — ownerId is never consulted. Additionally, an admin of tenant X can now delete records in tenant Y (true || false = true), which the old predicate denied. This is an authorization regression on the only access-control gate for deletion.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse errors, causing updateFontSize to overwrite corrupt settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a malformed `raw` (bad JSON or bad field types) propagated an error to callers, so `updateFontSize` (src/settings.ts:20) aborted before calling `save` and the stored settings were left intact. Now the error is converted into `{...DEFAULTS}`, indistinguishable from real settings: `updateFontSize` proceeds to `save(JSON.stringify(settings))`, silently persisting `theme: "light"` over whatever the user actually had whenever the stored blob is corrupt/truncated. Callers cannot distinguish 'parse failed' from 'settings legitimately are the defaults'.

findings.title: pageCount uses Math.floor, hiding the final partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: With Math.floor, pageCount(11, 10) returns 1 instead of 2, so any totalItems that is not an exact multiple of pageSize loses its last page; consumers paginating by this count will never surface the remaining items.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.

findings.title: artifacts fetched from 'verified' ref no longer match builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously artifacts were fetched at the same commit reported in builtFrom (build.ref(branch)). Now artifacts come from build.ref('verified'), which resolves a different ref; whenever 'verified' points at a different commit than the requested branch, the report claims the build came from commit X while listing artifacts produced at commit Y. Consumers correlating builtFrom with artifacts get an inconsistent report, and builds whose ref store has no 'verified' name may now fail or return unrelated artifacts where they previously succeeded.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit) so positive limit actually caps results
findings.whyItBreaks: The change drops `.slice(0, limit)`: for any positive limit, `return sorted` yields the entire reversed array, violating the documented 'at most `limit` entries' contract. The only caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9), calls recentEntries(all, 20) and copies page.length items — with the cap gone it emits all entries instead of a 20-item page, so every feed renders unbounded history.

findings.title: entry-count header reports unfiltered total after stale filtering
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest filters out stale entries for the row list but passes entries.length to headerLines. For any input containing a stale entry, `# entry-count:` reports a count larger than the number of rows actually emitted, so consumers parsing the header see a manifest that does not match its declared count.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws, breaking all callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's body was replaced with `throw new Error("always fails")`. The signature still promises `(input: string): string`, but no invocation can return — every call to `execute` now raises an exception instead of returning `input.toUpperCase()`. This is a total functional regression of the module's only export, not a reachable-error path.

findings.title: Viewer guard in isEligible dead-codes handle()'s read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` to isEligible means handle() now returns "rejected" for every viewer, so the existing `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` branch at src/handler.ts:25 is unreachable dead code. Before this change, an active viewer under the attempt cap was eligible and received "read-only"; now they are rejected outright. The unchanged downstream branch proves the contract was that viewers are handleable with read-only behavior, not ineligible — the guard rejects an action that was legitimately approvable on its own.

findings.title: Payment gate on shared canProceed blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Requiring order.payment === "paid" legitimately governs submitOrder, but not saveDraft. Substitution: order={state:"draft",payment:"missing"} previously returned true → saveDraft returned "saved"; now returns false → saveDraft returns "blocked". Users can no longer save a draft of an unpaid order — a legitimate action rejected by a predicate that should not govern it.

findings.title: Snapshot files resolved from 'stable' ref instead of the channel's head
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot records `commit: head` (headCommit of the requested channel) but builds `files` from `repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")`. The snapshot's file list therefore describes a different commit than `snapshot.commit` claims — for every channel other than one literally named 'stable', consumers see the channel's head commit paired with stable's file contents. It also makes publishing any channel fail if a 'stable' ref does not exist, since headCommit('stable') is called unconditionally.

findings.title: Honor the new `limit` parameter instead of hardcoded max_count
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature adds `limit=10`, promising callers control over the result count, but the body still iterates `range(max_count)` with `max_count = 10` at line 2 and never reads `limit`. Any caller passing e.g. `build('x', 3)` receives 10 items instead of 3 — the promised capping behavior affects the returned data and is not implemented.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but accepts negative and zero input
findings.whyItBreaks: The rename advertises a positivity guarantee (`parse_positive_int`), but the body is still plain `int(value)`, so `charge('-5')` silently returns -500 instead of rejecting. Callers trusting the name skip their own validation and can persist or report negative amounts as valid.

findings.title: apply_values mutates caller's DataFrame after dropping defensive copy
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `result = df.copy()` and writes with `df.loc[...] = value` directly on the caller's DataFrame. Previously the input was left untouched and a transformed copy was returned; now any caller that keeps using its original `df` after `apply_values(df, mapping)` sees the mapped values baked in, so repeated calls, comparisons against the original, or downstream reads of the unmodified frame silently observe mutated data. The function signature gives no hint of the in-place contract.

findings.title: Renaming ci.yml to docs/ci.md deletes the only GitHub Actions workflow
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only executes workflows located under .github/workflows/. This rename moves the repo's only workflow (lint + npm test on push/pull_request) to docs/ci.md, so CI silently stops running on every push and PR — nothing gates merges anymore. README.md line 5 still states 'CI runs lint and tests on every push', so the regression is invisible to readers, and docs/ci.md is raw workflow YAML, not usable documentation.

findings.title: parse_positive_int never enforces positivity; charge() emits negative/zero charges
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function promises a positive int, but `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` returns negative values unchanged (`"-5"` → -5) and maps parse failure to 0, indistinguishable from parsing `"0"`. The only caller `charge` (src/parse.rs:6) does no validation and multiplies by 100, so `charge("-5")` yields -500 (a negative charge/credit) and `charge("abc")` silently yields 0 — before the rename, `read_int` made no positivity promise callers could rely on; now the contract claims a guarantee the body does not implement.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves the Vec, breaking compilation at items.len()
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg! evaluates its argument by value and returns it; since the result is discarded, `items` is moved on line 2 and `items.len()` on line 3 fails to compile (E0382 use of moved value). Even if fixed to borrow, leftover dbg! also leaks item contents to stderr on every call.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against the pinned revision, not 'latest'
findings.whyItBreaks: buildChangeset resolves `from` from pinnedTag but now calls `store.readChangedPaths(latest)`, so the returned Changeset pairs `fromRevision: from` with a path list computed against a different revision. The interface contract on `fromRevision` (src/changeset.ts:7-8) states it is 'the revision the changed paths were computed against' and that 'consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision'. When `latest` has moved past `from`, any change between `from` and `latest` is silently absent from changedPaths, so replaying on top of `from` produces an incomplete/incorrect result — silent divergence that consumers cannot detect.

findings.title: Rename users.email breaks existing SELECT in src/query.sql
findings.whyItBreaks: After 0002 runs, the column `email` no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes `SELECT email FROM users;`, which will fail with an unknown-column error on every database that has applied this migration.

findings.title: Hardcoded live billing API key replaces BILLING_API_KEY env lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient() now embeds the literal key "bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0" in source, so the credential is committed to git history and shipped to anyone with repo or build access — a live billing secret leak. It also removes the `if (!key) throw` guard, so a misconfigured environment no longer fails fast; every deployment silently authenticates with the same leaked key instead of its own BILLING_API_KEY, and operators can no longer detect a missing configuration.

findings.title: Inverted isAdmin guard blocks admins and authorizes non-admins
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a purge required `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. The rewritten guard returns "forbidden" when `user.isAdmin` is true, so the only authorized callers (admins) are now rejected, while any non-admin can delete an archived project via `db.delete(project.id)` — an authorization bypass on a destructive operation plus a complete breakage of the admin workflow.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.

findings.title: startup() crashes on missing config instead of using defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when the file does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The removed fallback used to substitute {"workers": 1, "region": "us-east-1"}; now settings["workers"] is evaluated on None, raising TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable. A previously working missing-file path now crashes startup.

findings.title: Charge returns nil when gateway Submit fails, hiding payment failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a gw.Submit error was wrapped and returned (base pay/charge.go:14), so callers could detect and handle a failed charge. The diff replaces the return with log.Printf and falls through to `return nil`, so every caller of the exported Charge function observes a failed payment as a successful one — failure and success are indistinguishable, and callers may record, bill, or fulfill on a charge that never happened.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) ignores tenantId, so `settings:foo` is shared globally. Once tenant A fetches setting 'foo', tenant B's settingsFor(B, 'foo', ...) hits the same cache entry and receives tenant A's value — a cross-tenant data leak. invalidate(name) likewise now purges the entry for all tenants and can no longer target a single tenant.

findings.title: Decrement stock before awaiting save to prevent concurrent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads remaining at line 15, then suspends on `await this.store.save(...)` at line 17 before writing the decrement at line 18. Two concurrent reserve(sku) calls on a SKU with remaining=1 both read 1, both pass the <=0 guard, both persist `save(sku, 0)`, and both return true — one unit is sold twice. Previously reserve was synchronous, so the check and the decrement were atomic with respect to the event loop; the new await introduces the only possible interleaving point exactly between them.

findings.title: retry.ts still treats backoff() result as seconds, sleeps 1000x too long
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)). poll.ts was updated to use the value directly, but the other caller src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still computes `backoff(a) * 1000`. Every retry sleep is now 1000x longer: attempt 0 sleeps 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, and the cap yields 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Any failure entering retry() effectively stalls the job.

findings.title: Deferred f.Close() swallows the close error Save used to return
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function ended with `return f.Close()`, propagating close failures to the caller. Now `defer f.Close()` runs after `return w.Flush()` has already fixed the return value, so any error from Close is discarded. On filesystems where Close performs real write-back or reports delayed errors (NFS, FUSE, quota-limited or delayed-allocation filesystems where ENOSPC/EIO can surface at close), Save can return nil even though the file was not durably/completely written — the caller is told the save succeeded when it failed. Since Save is exported, every caller is forced to conflate a failed close with success; failure and success are no longer distinguishable.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds correctly returns half-open [start, end) bounds (its docstring says so), but page_window iterates range(start, end - 1), so the final row of every page is silently omitted. render_page and summarize both consume page_window, so rendered output loses one row per page — e.g. summarize(rows=[1,2,3], page_size=3) renders only rows 1 and 2, and a page containing a single row renders empty.

findings.title: Inverted TTL comparison serves expired entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `<` to `>` inverts the expiry check: when elapsed < ttlMs (entry still fresh) the new branch is false, so the entry is deleted and get() returns null; when elapsed > ttlMs (entry expired) the branch returns the stale value and the entry is never deleted. The cache now drops every fresh value on first read and serves expired values indefinitely.

findings.title: splice-during-forEach leaves consecutive done jobs unpruned
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach visits indices of the live array; splicing index i shifts later elements left while forEach advances to i+1, so the element that moved into index i is never checked. For [done, done, pending], index 0 is removed, iteration jumps to index 1 (now 'pending'), and the second done job survives in the result.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new filtered array and left the input untouched. The new code splices elements out of the passed-in array, so any caller that retains a reference to the original jobs list (e.g. to count removed jobs, reuse it, or iterate it elsewhere) observes it silently modified — a caller-visible contract change with no signature or doc update.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty input after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard means an empty array now computes `0 / 0` = NaN instead of the previously returned 0. Every caller that previously received a usable number now gets NaN, which silently propagates into sums, comparisons, and serialized output (NaN !== NaN breaks equality checks).

findings.title: busiest sorts the caller's array in place, mutating input order
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)` drops the defensive copy. `Array.prototype.sort` mutates in place, so callers that pass an array they still use (e.g., preserving display/insertion order, or reusing it for other aggregations) get their data silently reordered as a side effect of a read-only-looking query function.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator: default sort() orders scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically. For scores [9, 100], sort() yields [100, 9] ("100" < "9"), and reverse() yields [9, 100] — treated as descending when it is actually ascending. topPlayers then computes cutoff = scores[0] = 9 for n=1, so filter(score >= 9) keeps both players and slice(0,1) returns the score-9 player ahead of the true leader with 100. The previous code used (a, b) => b - a, a correct numeric descending sort. Any score set mixing magnitudes (e.g. single vs multi-digit, negatives, decimals) produces a wrong leaderboard.

findings.title: HMAC signature check uses timing-unsafe == instead of compare_digest
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates webhook signatures and gates handle() at app/webhook.py:14 (401 vs executing processor(payload)). Python's == on str short-circuits on the first differing byte and on length, leaking how much of the expected MAC an attacker-controlled given_signature matches. hmac.compare_digest existed precisely to make this comparison constant-time; reverting to == allows byte-by-byte signature forgery via response-timing measurement over repeated requests.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change all three statements ran inside `with db.transaction()`. Now the ledger INSERT commits when the `with` block exits, and `_apply_balances` executes afterward outside any transaction. If the debit UPDATE fails or the process dies between the two UPDATEs, the committed ledger records a transfer whose balances never moved (or a debit with no credit) — permanent inconsistent financial state that the old code rolled back atomically.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time instead of UTC, shifting billing dates
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new code uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. A timestamp like 2026-09-01T22:30:00Z produced '2026-09-01' before, but now yields '2026-09-02' on any host east of UTC (e.g. TZ=Asia/Taipei) and can yield '2026-08-31'/'2026-09-01' variations west of UTC. Billing day assignment becomes dependent on server/process TZ, producing different results across environments for identical input and silently reclassifying near-midnight usage into the wrong billing day.

findings.title: Memo key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile cache hits
findings.whyItBreaks: `key` changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account` while `readProfile` still accepts `tenant` as a parameter and the module-level `memo` Map persists across calls. After `readProfile('t1','acct',f)` caches t1's profile, `readProfile('t2','acct',f)` hits `memo.get('acct')` and returns tenant t1's `Profile` — including `tenant: 't1'` and t1's `displayName` — without ever calling `fetchProfile` for t2. Any consumer relying on the returned profile's tenant data gets another tenant's data (cross-tenant data exposure / wrong identity), and there is no way for callers to bypass or detect the wrong-tenant hit.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns "" indistinguishable from real value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw `missing: ${key}` when the key was absent (src/store.ts:4), so callers could distinguish 'key missing' from a stored empty string. The new catch-all maps that failure to "" — exactly the value a caller gets for a legitimately stored empty string — so failure and a real value are no longer distinguishable. The in-repo caller loadAll (src/store.ts:11-12) previously propagated the throw on the first missing key; it now silently produces "" entries in the result array, which downstream code would persist/report as real values. load is also exported, so every future caller is forced to conflate lookup failure with a legitimate result. The bare `catch` additionally swallows any unrelated throw inside the try, not just the missing-key error.

findings.title: Renaming timeoutMs to timeout silently disables the deadline for existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The public Config field `timeoutMs` was renamed to `timeout`. TypeScript callers break at compile time, but JavaScript callers still passing `{ timeoutMs: N }` get `config.timeout === undefined`, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is `NaN` and `Date.now() > NaN` is always false — the deadline check never fires and the timeout is silently ignored (loop always runs the full attempt count). The rename also drops the unit contract: `timeout` no longer tells callers the value is milliseconds.

findings.title: retryBackground treats `retries` as total attempts, so retries:0 never calls fn
findings.whyItBreaks: `for (let i = 0; i < config.retries; i++)` uses `retries` as the total number of invocations including the first. By the conventional meaning of the word, `retries: 0` should still execute `fn` once (zero re-tries); here `fn` is never invoked and the function returns silently. Config now carries two parallel count fields — `maxAttempts` (read by `retry`) and `retries` (read only by `retryBackground`) — so a caller must know which field each function reads, and the obvious value for `retries` produces a silent no-op.

findings.title: Exported retryBackground name promises async work but the body is synchronous
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name `retryBackground` promises non-blocking/background execution, but the body is a synchronous loop identical to `retry` — it blocks the caller's thread for up to `config.timeout` (unbounded per-iteration `fn()` latency times `retries` iterations) and returns void. A caller dispatching it as fire-and-forget background work stalls the event loop instead. It is also a verbatim reimplementation of `retry` with only the count field changed.

findings.title: retryBackground discards every fn() error and reports no failure signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception from `fn()` is caught and dropped (`catch { continue; }`), and after the loop exhausts all attempts the function returns void with no signal. This is an exported/public swallow site: every eventual caller is forced to conflate total failure with success — there is no return value, no rethrow, and no log to distinguish them.

findings.title: Field renders length label instead of the actual value
findings.whyItBreaks: `defaultValue` is set to `len=${value.length}` rather than `value`, so the input displays e.g. `len=5` instead of the field's content. The real value is never shown, and since the input is uncontrolled, the user's edit operates on the `len=...` text — the original value is lost entirely.

findings.title: `value.length` is invalid on the new `string | number` union
findings.whyItBreaks: The prop type was widened to `string | number`, but `number` has no `.length`. `value.length` is a compile error under `tsc` (TS2339: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'number'), and under type-stripping transpilers (esbuild/babel) it silently produces `len=undefined` at runtime for every numeric value — precisely the inputs the widened type now admits.

findings.title: Deploy step prints secrets.TOKEN to CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step does `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` with TOKEN bound from secrets.TOKEN. GitHub log masking only replaces exact secret value matches and is explicitly best-effort — multiline secrets, transformed/encoded forms, or values that collide with other log text can leak into persisted workflow logs, which are downloadable artifacts. GitHub's own guidance is to never print secrets. The step also serves no functional purpose (no deploy command consumes TOKEN), so it exposes the credential for zero benefit.

score.error: malformed critic output: finding was not in the candidate review

findings.title: Dropping '-s read-only' lets codex exec run commands with ambient sandbox policy
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns 'codex exec' to run a model-generated agent. Before this change it forced '--sandbox read-only', so model-generated shell commands could not write. Now the sandbox falls back to whatever the caller's ~/.codex/config.toml or profile specifies — including 'danger-full-access' or an approval mode that may auto-approve in non-interactive contexts. In an automation runner (needlefish), a prompt-injected or misbehaving agent could write/delete files in the reviewed repo or elsewhere on disk, where previously it was read-only.

findings.title: Diff against base tip instead of merge-base includes unrelated base changes
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is either PR_BASE_SHA (in GitHub Actions the natural value is pull_request.base.sha, i.e. the base branch tip) or the merge-base fallback. When PR_BASE_SHA is a base tip that has advanced past the PR's merge-base, `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff: it includes every commit that landed on the base branch since the PR branched, shown as reverse hunks, and changedFileSet() (git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD, line 56) lists files the PR never touched. The reviewer model receives a corrupted patch, and findings anchored to those non-PR files make the GitHub reviews API reject the payload (422), silently downgrading to a review with no inline comments via the catch at line ~97. The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` was exactly the standard three-dot fix for this.

findings.title: Patch diffs literal HEAD while commit_id/bundle report headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff previously used the resolved `headSha` (PR_HEAD_SHA || rev-parse HEAD). It now uses literal "HEAD", so when PR_HEAD_SHA is set to a commit that differs from the checked-out HEAD — the exact override scenario the env var exists for, e.g. a stale or differently-fetched checkout — bundle.headSha and the review's commit_id claim headSha while patch/changedFiles were computed from a different tree. The review then describes and anchors comments against a commit it did not actually diff.

findings.title: Revert to replacer functions: string replacements reinterpret '$' patterns in patch content
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats special patterns in a string replacement: '$$' collapses to '$', '$&' re-inserts the matched placeholder text ({{PATCH}}/{{BUNDLE}}/{{FINDINGS}} remain in the prompt), "$'" inserts the entire post-match prompt suffix, and "$`" inserts the prefix. The replacement strings here are JSON.stringify(bundle) and bundle.patch — both contain arbitrary diff text where '$$' (shell PIDs, Makefile escapes, JS libs) and '$''/ '$&' (Ruby/Perl post-match vars) are common. The previous function replacer `() => str` returns the value verbatim with no '$' interpretation; this PR removes that protection, so affected patches silently corrupt the review and critic prompts fed to runCodex, producing wrong review output.

findings.title: Deleted Number.isFinite guards let NaN leak into Finding.lineStart/lineEnd
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding({lineStart: "abc"}) now returns lineStart: NaN (and lineEnd: NaN via `raw.lineEnd ?? raw.lineStart`). The old code threw on non-finite line numbers. NaN violates the Finding type's `lineStart: number` contract, serializes to `null` in JSON.stringify output, and defeats any downstream `lineStart <= 0` or range check — a malformed finding now ships corrupted coordinates that are neither a valid line nor a rejected error.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently fabricates findings from malformed entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a malformed finding either threw (strict=true) or was dropped (strict=false). Now raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) unconditionally converts every malformed entry into a plausible-looking finding: invalid severity defaults to "P1" (the severity that typically blocks merge), missing title becomes "Untitled finding", missing file becomes "", and missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix become empty strings. Callers can no longer distinguish a model-emitted real finding from garbage — the exported API contract forces failure-as-value. Additionally `category` is checked without the trim()/case-normalization that `severity` still gets, so e.g. "Security" or "runtime " silently downgrades to "bug".

findings.title: gh pr view loses repo context; dispatch path yields empty refs and wrong checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On `workflow_dispatch`, EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE are empty, so the else branch runs `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"`. With `-R "$REPO"` removed and no `GH_REPO` env set (`gh` only honors `GH_REPO`, not GitHub's `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`), gh must infer the repo from the local git remote — but this step runs before `actions/checkout`, so the workdir has no `.git`. `gh` fails inside the command substitution; `echo` still writes `head=`/`base=` (empty) to GITHUB_OUTPUT, so the step 'succeeds' and `actions/checkout` receives an empty `ref`, checking out the default branch instead of the PR head, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty for the review run.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed input as an empty passing review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, non-object input, a non-string summary, or missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks threw 'malformed review output: ...', so callers could catch the error and retry or escalate. Now every malformed shape is coerced to {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} — byte-identical to a legitimate all-clear review. Any consumer (retry loop, verdict classifier, needs_human fallback) cannot distinguish a truncated/garbage model response from a genuine pass and will treat review failure as approval.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch runs check out the default branch, not the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is null, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` resolves to github.ref (the repo default branch). The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step handled this by calling `gh pr view $PR_NUM --json headRefOid`. A manual dispatch now silently checks out and installs the default branch instead of the requested PR, so the tool reviews the wrong code.

findings.title: PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty on workflow_dispatch runs
findings.whyItBreaks: github.event.pull_request.base.sha and .head.sha are only populated for pull_request events; on workflow_dispatch they interpolate as empty strings (no `||` fallback here). The previous step resolved both via `gh pr view $PR_NUM --json baseRefOid,headRefOid`. The CLI therefore receives empty SHAs for the diff range, so dispatch runs either fail or review nothing — a regression of an explicitly supported trigger. BASE_REF similarly hard-falls back to 'main' regardless of the PR's actual base branch.

findings.title: git diff output now capped at ~1MiB, breaking reviews of large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Node's spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024 (1 MiB). The removed option raised it to 64 MiB. `git(args...)` at line 100 runs `git diff baseSha HEAD`, whose output is the entire review payload — diffs over ~1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, large PRs, vendored changes) are routine. Verified: spawnSync with default options on >1MiB stdout returns status=null with error ENOBUFS; the `res.status !== 0` check then throws 'git diff ... failed: ' with an empty stderr message, so the whole `runLocal` path aborts. Previously it succeeded up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Errored review posts neutral conclusion that satisfies required checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, the check run is posted with conclusion "neutral" while the summary claims "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." GitHub treats a check-run conclusion of neutral as satisfied for branch-protection required checks, so if the "Needlefish" check run is required, a crashed/errored review no longer blocks merge — the gate is fail-open instead of fail-closed. The carrier text contradicts the posted conclusion, and previously "failure" correctly rejected.

findings.title: headSha uses PR head SHA, which check-runs rejects for fork PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha now comes from pr.head.sha instead of the local checkout HEAD. For fork PRs (pull_request or pull_request_target), the fork's head commit does not exist in the base repository, so POST repos/{base}/check-runs with that head_sha returns 422. The throw is caught by the outer catch, which calls postCheck again with the same bad head_sha, throws again, and runGithub rejects — no check run is ever posted and the process exits on an unhandled rejection. Previously the local HEAD (merge/head commit present in the base repo checkout) always validated.

findings.title: Review tool now executes from untrusted PR head with write token
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow explicitly implemented a trusted-tool pattern: the reviewer was checked out from frankekn/needlefish@main while only the PR head was untrusted, so a PR could not control its own review. This diff deletes that second checkout and runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR head checkout itself. Every file executed (src/cli.ts, package.json, the lockfile-resolved dependency tree installed by `pnpm install`) is now fully controlled by the PR author. The step exports `GH_TOKEN` for a job whose permissions grant `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, so a malicious PR can self-approve, forge the review verdict, write arbitrary checks/comments, and persist code on the self-hosted runner. The `if` guard only restricts to same-repo heads and does not prevent a collaborator's PR from controlling its own review; `workflow_dispatch` bypasses the head-repo check entirely while `gh pr view` can resolve any PR's head SHA.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization; "p0"-style input now collapses to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed String(...).trim().toUpperCase() tolerated case/whitespace in model-produced JSON. Now any severity not exactly matching "P0"|"P1"|"P2"|"P3" — e.g. "p0", " P2 ", or unrecognized values like "critical" — falls through to the new "P3" default (was "P1"). A real high-severity finding emitted in lowercase is silently reported as the lowest severity via normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132), which can suppress or deprioritize it in any downstream verdict/sort/gating that reads severity.

findings.title: Child codex process now inherits GitHub tokens deleted env scrub removed
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously runCodex built a sanitized env copy and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync. After this change spawnSync is called without an `env` option, so the child inherits process.env verbatim, including those tokens. This function spawns `codex exec` to run a prompt against a repo (a PR-review tool — the prompt/repo content is attacker-influenced). The agent inside codex can read its own environment (`env`, `printenv GH_TOKEN`) even under `-s read-only`; the token value can then be embedded in the returned last message, which flows back into review output/comments — disclosing a live credential. The scrub was deliberate defense-in-depth for exactly this leakage class, and the diff removes it with no replacement.

findings.title: Restore same-repo guard: fork PRs get RCE on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing preventing fork PRs from reaching this job. Without it, any external user can open a PR and have their code run on a self-hosted runner: `actions/checkout` fetches the attacker-controlled head SHA, `pnpm install` executes install scripts from the PR's modified package.json/lockfile, and `tsx src/cli.ts` runs the PR's own source. Self-hosted runners are not ephemeral — this enables persistent runner compromise, theft of cached credentials/tools, and lateral movement. The `pull_request` event (unlike `pull_request_target`) was specifically safe to combine with checking out PR code only because the guard kept the trust boundary at same-repo actors; the GITHUB_TOKEN being downgraded to read-only for forks does not mitigate runner compromise.

findings.title: Removed coverage backstop lets changed files escape deep review entirely
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block pushed a tail hotspot containing every changed file not covered by the selected hotspots. Coverage was computed AFTER `slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`, so it caught both files the map pass never assigned AND files inside hotspots truncated beyond index 5. With it gone, any file the map pass omits — or that lives in a dropped hotspot — gets zero deep review and nothing records the gap, so a large PR can be reported as fully reviewed while files were never examined.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks are discarded via hardcoded empty array
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review's `res.residual_risks` was previously accumulated into `residuals` and passed to the critic in `candidateMerged.residual_risks`, so blocks:true risks reached the critic and the verdict. Now the loop drops them and `residual_risks: []` is sent instead — a deep pass that reports 'could not verify X, blocks' has that signal silently erased before the critic sees the candidate.

findings.title: Single deep-pass failure now aborts the whole large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed try/catch recorded 'DEEP PASS FAILED' in checked and appended a blocking residual risk, then continued reviewing remaining hotspots. Now any throw from `runCodex`/`extractJson`/`normalizeReview` inside the loop propagates out of reviewLarge, discarding every other hotspot's results and failing the entire review on one malformed or transient LLM response.

findings.title: Dedup key no longer distinguishes findings with different root causes
findings.whyItBreaks: The key dropped `norm(f.whyItBreaks).slice(0, 80)` and norm now truncates titles at 60 chars. Two distinct findings at the same file/lineStart/category whose normalized titles collide (identical, or differing only after char 60) but describe different defects now collapse into one, silently dropping the lower-severity distinct issue.

findings.title: Focus option silently ignored for large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: bundle.focus is still a field on Bundle and still reaches the model on the small path (reviewSmall serializes the entire bundle into {{BUNDLE}}), but this diff removes it from both the map bundle and the deep prompt ({{FOCUS}} replace deleted). On the large path the user's requested focus now influences neither hotspot selection nor any deep pass, so `focus` silently does nothing exactly on the PRs where scoping matters most. Additionally, if prompts/deep.md still contains the {{FOCUS}} placeholder, it now ships literally to the model.

findings.title: formatDuration renders '60s' when remainder rounds up to a full minute
findings.whyItBreaks: Seconds are rounded after splitting off minutes, so when (ms % 60000) >= 59500 the seconds field rounds to 60 without incrementing minutes. 59999ms renders '60s' instead of '1m 0s', and 119999ms renders '1m 60s' instead of '2m 0s'. The old code rounded total seconds first, guaranteeing seconds < 60.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0, breaking its positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger('0', label)` now returns 0 instead of throwing. The exported function name and its own error message (`${label} requires a positive integer`, still thrown for negatives) both promise a strictly positive result — callers relying on that validation receive a value the contract says is impossible. If zero is now intended for some input, the carrier (name + error text) must be updated or a separate parser added; as written the body silently contradicts its public contract.
